In the school lift, Charu hesitated. “Pranav, I have to tell you something. People are saying you copied in the maths test.” Pranav's ears went hot. “I didn't.” “I know. But it's on the class group.”

All day he watched faces. Two girls stopped talking when he passed. A boy in the corridor smirked. Pranav stared at his shoes and counted tiles. He couldn't tell who had started it; anyone might have.

At lunch he sat behind the library shelves for ten minutes, wishing he could vanish. When he came out, Charu was waiting. “I'll come with you to talk to Mrs. Kulkarni,” she said. “Right now.” “Now?” “Now.”

qa.q: Where did Charu tell Pranav about the rumour?
qa.a: Charu told Pranav about the rumour in the school lift.

qa.q: What was Pranav feeling as watching faces all day?
qa.a: Pranav felt hot shame and fear of every glance, unable to tell who had started the story.

qa.q: What choice did Charu make that helped Pranav?
qa.a: Charu offered to go with Pranav to Mrs. Kulkarni right away.

qa.q: What might Charu have been feeling while telling Pranav about the rumour?
qa.a: Charu probably felt nervous and worried for Pranav but loyal enough to tell the truth.

grounding: A teenager learns that a false story about them is spreading, feels hot shame and fear of every glance, and cannot tell who started it.

passage:
Nikita, his older sister, sat on the edge of Akash's bed.

“Akash, you need to hear something.”

“What?”

“A girl from my tuition class says there's a story going round your school. That you copied a friend's homework and blamed someone else.”

“What? That's not true.” His voice cracked. “Who said that?”

“I don't know. It's just going round.”

“So everyone thinks...” Akash pulled the blanket up. “I can't go tomorrow. I'll just disappear.”

Mummy stood in the doorway holding a dishcloth. “Akash, come here. Whatever it is, tell me.” He told her everything. She listened, then took out her phone. “I'll call your class teacher tonight. And you're not walking in alone tomorrow.”

Nikita nodded. “I'll stand next to you at the gate.”

qa.q: Who will walk in with Akash tomorrow?
qa.a: Nikita will stand next to Akash at the gate and walk in with Akash.

qa.q: Why did Akash say he would just disappear?
qa.a: Akash felt shame and fear that everyone at school believed the false story, so hiding felt like the only escape.

qa.q: What did Mummy do the same evening?
qa.a: Mummy listened to Akash and said she would call the class teacher that night.

qa.q: What might Nikita have felt when delivering the news?
qa.a: Nikita probably felt worried and protective, unsure how Akash would react but wanting Akash to hear it from family.

grounding: A teenager learns that a false story about them is spreading, feels shame and a wish to disappear, and cannot tell who started it.

In the kasba, news travelled faster than the bus. By Tuesday, Tushar pulled Raghav aside at the tea stall. “People are saying you took money from the temple donation box. The Rath Yatra collection.”
Raghav felt the blood rush to his face. “What? I only helped count it!”
“I know. But Pintu's mother is telling everyone.”
All the way home, Raghav felt eyes on him. The shopkeeper looked twice. Two aunties stopped talking. He wanted to disappear into the ground. Who even started it?
At home, he told his father everything. His father put down his newspaper, said, “I believe you,” and that evening walked with Raghav to the temple committee to ask for the collection records to be checked in front of everyone.

qa.q: What were people saying Raghav took?
qa.a: Money from the temple donation box, the Rath Yatra collection.

qa.q: What was Raghav feeling on the way home?
qa.a: He felt ashamed and afraid of every glance, wishing he could disappear into the ground.

qa.q: How did Raghav's father respond, and why did it help?
qa.a: He believed Raghav and went with him that evening to ask for the records to be checked openly, which gives facts a chance against the rumour.

qa.q: How might Tushar have felt telling Raghav about the rumour?
qa.a: Tushar was probably uneasy but loyal, wanting a friend to know even though it was hard to say.

grounding: Shows a teenager learning a false story about him is spreading, feeling shame and fear of every glance, unsure who started it.

passage:
Rosa noticed it first on Monday in her school in Barcelona: people went quiet when she walked in. By lunch, her friend Carla told her. “They're saying you copied the maths test from Oskar.”
“I sat by the window! Oskar was three rows away!”
“I know. I don't know who started it.”
All afternoon Rosa kept her head down. Every laugh seemed to be about her. She wanted to go home and never come back.
At home she told her mother, who listened, then said, “You didn't do this, and you shouldn't have to carry it.” She emailed Rosa's maths teacher that evening. The teacher replied before dinner: the tests had been checked, Rosa's was her own work, and she would speak to the class.

qa.q: Where did Rosa say she sat during the test?
qa.a: She sat by the window.

qa.q: What was Rosa feeling all afternoon?
qa.a: She felt ashamed and afraid, as if every laugh was about her, wanting to go home and never come back.

qa.q: How did Rosa's mother help?
qa.a: She listened, told Rosa she didn't have to carry it, and emailed the teacher that evening, who replied before dinner.

qa.q: How might Oskar feel about the rumour?
qa.a: Oskar may feel awkward or annoyed, dragged into a false story he had nothing to do with.

grounding: Shows a teenager discovering a false cheating rumour about her, feeling shame and fear, unable to find who started it.

passage:
At the coaching institute's hostel, Akash noticed the change in one evening. Boys stopped chatting when he walked into the common room. Someone muttered “spy” behind him.
His classmate Swati found him in the library. “Akash, people are saying you told the warden about the phones. Everyone's angry.”
“I didn't! I don't even know who has phones!”
“I believe you. But it's everywhere.”
Akash's face burned. He skipped dinner and sat in his room, jumping at every footstep. He couldn't even guess who had started it.
At nine, he went to the institute counsellor's office. She listened, said, “You don't have to handle this alone,” and spoke to the warden that same night to make clear no student had reported anything.

qa.q: What did someone mutter behind Akash?
qa.a: Someone muttered "spy" behind him.

qa.q: What was Akash feeling sitting in his room?
qa.a: He felt ashamed and frightened, jumping at every footstep and unable to guess who started the rumour.

qa.q: What did Akash do that helped, and what did the counsellor do?
qa.a: He went to the counsellor that evening; she listened, told him he wasn't alone and spoke to the warden the same night.

qa.q: How might Swati have felt telling Akash about the rumour?
qa.a: Swati was likely worried for Akash and uncomfortable, but loyal enough to warn Akash and say so.

grounding: Shows a teenager in a hostel learning a false rumour about him is spreading, feeling shame and fear of every glance.

Baljeet,
You're the only one I can tell, since you're in Delhi now.
Since Monday, everyone at school is saying I copied in the prelims. That I had answers on my wrist. I didn't. I scored 92 because I spent the whole Diwali break on past papers. You KNOW I did; you were on video call with me half the time.
I don't know who started it. Could be anyone. Now when someone looks at me in the corridor my face goes hot and I want to sink into the floor. Yesterday Ritu and Sameer stopped talking when I sat down. I keep practising what I'd say if someone asked me straight out. Nobody does. They just whisper.
Uday
PS: After writing this I showed it to Appa. He read it twice, said this is not my fault, and emailed my class teacher tonight to ask for a meeting tomorrow.

qa.q: What did Uday score in the prelims?
qa.a: Uday scored 92.

qa.q: How does Uday feel walking through the corridor now?
qa.a: Uday feels hot shame and fear of every glance, wishing to sink into the floor.

qa.q: Why was showing the letter to Appa a good step?
qa.a: An adult could act the same day, reassuring Uday and asking the school to deal with a rumour Uday can't fight alone.

qa.q: How might Baljeet feel reading this from Delhi?
qa.a: Baljeet may feel angry on Uday's behalf and helpless from far away, having seen the studying on video calls.

grounding: Shows a teenager who learns a false cheating rumour about them is spreading, feeling shame and fear of every glance without knowing who started it.
